A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the myoglobin of the red muscles of mammals, birds and fish, and the hemoglobin of red blood cells, function to buffer the intracellular oxygen pressure and to provide a mechanism for rapid, reversible, and efficient transport of oxygen between the site of oxygen entry to the muscle cell (capillary) and the site of oxygen utilization (mitochondrial matrix)
myoglobin functions as a buffer for oxygen in the sarcoplasm, a buffer that is capable of responding rapidly and reversibly to changes in oxygen supply and demand.
myoglobin is a critical component of the intracellular oxygen transport and diffusion system of the muscle cell.
The main takeaway from our work is that
myoglobin, a hemeprotein of 17 kD, is an important player in oxygen supply and demand in red muscles.
the sarcoplasmic volume average oxygen pressure in red muscle is near 3 torrs and that this pressure is maintained in the face of sustained changes in oxygen utilization.
the sarcoplasmic compartment in red muscle is a very efficient, highly integrated system for oxygen delivery to the mitochondria.
